evals.prompt: I run partnerships at Kelver, a workflow automation vendor doing about $38k ACV, sales-led, mid-market moving upmarket. We have nine technology alliance candidates on the list and two alliance managers, so realistically three alliances next year. I already built a scorecard: brand strength, market size, account overlap, exec relationship, and revenue potential, each at 20%, everyone scored 1-5. Top of the sheet right now is Northwind Cloud at 4.8 (that is the hyperscaler, our CEO golfs with their VP), then Piedmont Analytics at 4.4, then Solvexa Data at 3.2. Integration estimates I have: Northwind 7 manager-months, Piedmont 6, Solvexa 4, and the other six range from 2 to 5. Goal is partner-sourced enterprise pipeline. Can you turn this into a shortlist I can take to our VP of Sales next Tuesday?
evals.expected_output: A rebuilt ranking that rejects the equal-weight sheet, anchors weights on complementarity and compatibility with written justifications, divides value by effort, draws the capacity line on summed effort rather than the headcount of three, runs a sensitivity re-rank, and ends with explicit verdicts including at least one candidate left off.
expectations: Rejects the equal 20% weight distribution outright rather than tuning the numbers inside it
States that every weight must carry a written one-line justification
Names resource complementarity and organizational compatibility as the two criteria that should carry the highest weight
Points out that neither complementarity nor compatibility appears anywhere in the user's five existing criteria
Flags brand strength and exec relationship, together 40% of the sheet, as logo halo and relationship criteria that crowd out fit
Caps account overlap as one input rather than leaving it as an equal share of the ranking spine
Introduces an effort column and ranks candidates on value divided by effort
States the ranking order explicitly as value divided by effort, then value composite, then logo attractiveness
Shows that Northwind Cloud's 7 manager-months move its position once effort divides value, rather than leaving it first
Draws the capacity line on summed effort estimates rather than on the headcount number of three
Runs a sensitivity check shifting each weight plus or minus 20% and reports which positions hold and which flip
Applies a tie band of roughly 5% and refuses to treat a sub-5% composite gap as decisive
Scores the CEO-connected Northwind Cloud on the same sheet as every other candidate rather than protecting or excluding it
Ends with at least one candidate not making the shortlist, each non-shortlisted candidate carrying an explicit verdict
Asks for the missing interview inputs (existing alliance portfolio, data available per candidate, sign-off owner) before finalizing the table

evals.prompt: Follow-up on our alliance shortlist at Kelver. Piedmont Analytics came out highest on the scorecard at 4.4, but legal came back and said Piedmont has no SOC 2 Type II, their last attestation lapsed 14 months ago, and they had a customer data exposure incident in 2024 that they disclosed late. The alliance needs us to push customer records to them. Our VP wants to keep them in the shortlist and just add 'security posture' as a criterion at 15% weight so the sheet reflects it. Piedmont would still come out second even scoring a 1 there. Can you rework the scorecard that way?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to convert the security failure into a weighted criterion, removal of Piedmont from the ranked list on the gate, the evidence cited, conditional-go named as the only route back, and the shortlist and capacity line redrawn.
expectations: Refuses to convert security posture into a weighted scorecard criterion
States that must-pass gates live outside the tradeable score
Removes Piedmont Analytics from the ranked list on the gate failure rather than re-ranking it lower
States explicitly that a high composite score cannot buy a candidate past a gate
Names the specific evidence behind the gate decision: the lapsed attestation, the late-disclosed incident, and the customer-record data-sharing requirement
Identifies the failed gate as the security and compliance posture gate within a defined must-pass gate set
Offers conditional-go as the only route back, tied to a named condition and a deadline, rather than to a scored position
Lists the other must-pass gates the remaining candidates must clear, including financial viability, legal or antitrust exposure, exit path, and the three-laws screen
Explains that scoring and socializing a candidate before its security or legal gate is what makes a gate tradeable in the first place
Records the gate decision with its evidence inside the memo rather than parking it in a compliance annex
Does not average or blend the security concern into any composite score
Redraws the shortlist and the capacity line after the removal rather than promoting the next-highest value score by default

evals.prompt: Vantiq Systems here, we make field-service scheduling software. Our CPO says our biggest gap is predictive maintenance; we have no ML capability and no plan to build one. Six alliance candidates. Five are straightforward integration partners, 3 to 4 manager-months each, all would ship inside a quarter. The sixth is Orrin Labs, whose anomaly-detection engine would actually close the gap, but it needs them to expose a streaming inference endpoint they do not have yet, and we would need to build an event pipeline on our side. Their roadmap has the endpoint dated for Q3 next year; ours has the pipeline in the same half. Orrin would be about 9 manager-months. We have 14 manager-months total. My ranking has Orrin dead last on value-per-effort. Is that right?
evals.expected_output: An explanation that the ratio structurally starves the deep co-innovation candidate, confirmation that both dependencies are dated on the two parties' own roadmaps, promotion of Orrin by reserving capacity before scoring rather than by adding composite points, and co-innovation plus adoption-chain risk scored explicitly.
expectations: Names the value-per-effort ratio as structurally underweighting a candidate that is both expensive and strong
Identifies Orrin Labs as the deep co-innovation candidate in this list
Ties the promotion decision to the stated goal being product-gap fill rather than pipeline
Checks whether the unshipped dependency sits on the two parties' own dated roadmaps rather than a third party's
Confirms both the Orrin endpoint and the Vantiq pipeline carry dates, and treats that as the condition making the candidate promotable
States that an undated dependency would earn a recycle rather than a reserved capacity slot
Promotes Orrin by reserving a slice of capacity before scoring starts, not by adding points to its composite score
States that adding points to the composite would be the false precision the sensitivity analysis exists to undo
Spends the reserved co-innovation slot inside the 14 manager-month budget rather than on top of it
Scores co-innovation risk for Orrin as a named risk category, measuring how much of the value depends on an unshipped roadmap
Scores adoption-chain risk, asking which intermediaries must act before the end customer sees the value
Keeps Orrin's raw value-per-effort position visible rather than rewriting the ratio to justify the promotion
States how much capacity is left for the five integration candidates after Orrin's reserved slot

evals.prompt: We are Brackenly, a 40-person devtools company. Two candidates left after gates. One is Helixon, a big observability platform: we would list in their marketplace and build on their agent SDK, and about 70% of the joint value depends on that SDK. They shipped a first-party feature last quarter that overlaps maybe 60% with what we do, and their marketplace terms let them feature their own modules above third-party ones. The other is Tunstall Metrics: small, no product overlap with us, no prior relationship, roadmap heading straight at a segment we also want, and their CEO has said publicly that partnerships are 'a distraction'. But their tech fit is excellent and the integration is easy. Which do we back?
evals.expected_output: Platform envelopment named and scored for Helixon with staged commitment and a dependency ceiling rather than a veto, relational and performance risk scored separately for both, Tunstall flagged as high relational risk, and the risk composite shown beside value and effort.
expectations: Names platform envelopment as the specific risk Helixon carries
Cites the warning signs present: adjacent first-party features shipped, marketplace terms permitting self-preferencing, and value sitting in a thin replicable layer
States that high envelopment risk does not forbid the alliance
Requires staged commitment, contractual safeguards, and a stated dependency ceiling in the memo if Helixon proceeds
Scores relational risk and performance risk separately rather than collapsing them into one risk number
Identifies Tunstall Metrics as high relational risk, citing the competing roadmap, the absence of prior ties, and the publicly stated posture against partnerships
States that relational risk is mitigated by governance and staged commitment, not by enthusiasm or tech fit
States that performance risk is mitigated by pilots and milestone gates
States that a candidate high on both relational and performance risk is a kill or a small staged pilot, never a flagship bet
Shows the risk composite beside the value and effort columns rather than in an annex read after the decision
Names which risk drives the gap between the two candidates rather than presenting them as tied
States what mitigation would close that gap
Refuses to rank the two on tech fit and integration ease alone

evals.prompt: I head brand partnerships at Solane, a premium skincare brand. We are the high-end one in our category, average basket 95 euros. I have eleven partnership candidates for next year: four creator partnerships, three brand co-brands, two retail-media tie-ups, two podcast sponsorships. Budget covers maybe four. My agency sent audience overlap numbers and follower counts for all eleven and ranked them by reach. Top of their list is Marisse Bell, 2.1M followers, 48% audience overlap with us, but I have heard nothing about whether her numbers are real. Second is a co-brand with Halvern, a luxury fragrance house even more prestigious than us. Can you build me the ranking?
evals.expected_output: Fraud and brand-safety screens run pass/fail before scoring, brand fit named as the B2C fit construct, the high-esteem dilution warning applied to Solane in the Halvern pairing, reach capped as one input, and the same method spine as the B2B version with verdicts and a capacity line.
expectations: Runs creator fraud vetting as a pass/fail screen before any scoring, not as a scored criterion
Treats Marisse Bell's unverified follower base as unscreened rather than pre-screened
Requires an audience audit from a fraud-screening tool as the evidence behind that gate
Names brand safety as a second pass/fail gate for this candidate list
Names brand fit or attitude congruence as the core fit construct on the B2C side
States that attitude spillover between paired brands runs in both directions and not symmetrically
Warns that as the high-esteem brand Solane is the more exposed party in the Halvern co-brand, rather than the automatic beneficiary
Models at least one negative-spillover scenario per shortlisted candidate and what it would cost Solane
Caps audience overlap as one input rather than letting the agency's reach ranking be the ranking spine

States that the method spine, including staged gates, justified weights, sensitivity analysis, the capacity line, and the memo shape, is identical to the B2B version rather than inventing a separate B2C method
Demands incrementality-tested metrics rather than vanity reach figures
Scores effort per candidate and ranks on value against effort rather than on reach
Issues a verdict per candidate drawn from go, conditional-go, recycle, hold, and kill
Draws a capacity line and leaves below-the-line candidates with explicit re-entry triggers

evals.prompt: Writing the exec summary for our alliance shortlist at Carrowmore Software. I want to open with something that lands. I have two numbers from a partner-ops platform's report: '70% of alliances fail' and 'deals are 53% more likely to close when a partner is involved'. I also found a McKinsey survey saying 70% of alliances underperform. They all point the same direction, so I am going to lead with the 70% failure rate and use the 53% to justify the headcount ask. Draft me that paragraph.
evals.expected_output: A paragraph that refuses the single settled failure rate, presents the published spread and the lower re-analysis figures, separates underperformance from failure, downgrades the 53% claim to the vendor's own network figure, flags provenance on every number, and substitutes the peer-reviewed alliance-function finding for the headcount argument.
expectations: Refuses to state a single settled alliance failure rate
Presents the published spread of roughly 20% to 80% depending on how failure is defined
Cites the credible re-analysis putting failure nearer 25-30%
Notes the lower 18-20% figure for firms that have an alliance-management function
Traces the widely repeated 60-70% phrasing to the 2007 Harvard Business Review piece by Hughes and Weiss
States that this source cites no study, sample, or definition behind the figure
Distinguishes the McKinsey survey as measuring underperformance and need for restructuring, not outright failure
Notes the McKinsey survey's small base of roughly 30 companies
Identifies the 53% close-rate figure as a self-reported vendor survey of roughly 500 professionals
Contrasts it against the same vendor's own network data showing roughly an 11.7% win-rate lift
Recommends quoting the smaller, harder 11.7% figure if either is used at all
Attaches a provenance flag to every number kept in the memo, distinguishing peer-reviewed, analyst, vendor first-party, and vendor survey
Offers the Kale, Dyer and Singh finding of 63% versus 50% alliance success with a dedicated alliance function, across 1,572 alliances, as the defensible basis for the headcount ask

evals.prompt: Board meeting is Thursday morning. It is Tuesday afternoon and I have maybe two hours on this, no analyst, and I cannot pull RevOps for an overlap report. Three candidates: Aldwyn Networks, Fennimore Cloud, Brightsea AI. The board wants to know which one we sign this quarter. We have one alliance manager. Give me the scorecard.
evals.expected_output: The scorecard dropped under the effort ceiling and replaced by gates plus effort to first value, the full gate set run on all three rather than staged, reach-led criteria deleted outright with the reason stated, a capacity line still fixed, verdicts still issued, and candidate facts flagged unverified.
expectations: Removes the weighted scorecard entirely rather than producing one under the two-hour ceiling
Ranks instead on the must-pass gates plus effort to first value
States explicitly in the output that the scorecard was dropped and why
Runs the full gate set on all three candidates rather than staging desk checks ahead of expensive reviews
Explains that staging saves nothing on a longlist of three
Deletes reach-led criteria outright given no overlap dataset and no audience-audit budget
States the deletion reasoning: stripped of the dataset, reach-led leaves only market size and brand
Names each deleted option and its reason rather than demoting it to the bottom of a menu
Fixes a capacity line from the single alliance manager before recommending anything
Issues a verdict per candidate drawn from go, conditional-go, recycle, hold, and kill
Flags the candidate facts as user-supplied and unverified rather than presenting them as checked

evals.prompt: Second time around on this. Last quarter I brought a ranked alliance list to our steering committee and they reopened it. The CRO said the weights were 'made up' and we spent 90 minutes arguing about whether integration depth should count more than account overlap. Nothing got signed. We are re-running it in six weeks for the FY plan, and this scorecard is going to get re-run at every portfolio review after that. Seven candidates, four alliance-manager slots. Same committee, same CRO. How do I keep this from happening again?
evals.expected_output: Formal weight elicitation promoted above the justified-weights default for this specific situation, best-worst method named and preferred over AHP, its cost and what it actually buys stated plainly, and the sensitivity re-rank named as the artifact that survives the argument.
expectations: Promotes formal weight elicitation above the default of individually justified weights for this situation
Names the best-worst method as the elicitation technique to use
Prefers best-worst method over AHP, citing fewer pairwise comparisons and less rank-reversal exposure

Names the conditions that promote it: the weights themselves being what the room argues about, a sign-off owner who distrusts the sheet, a committee that has already reopened a ranking, and a scorecard that will be re-run at every portfolio review
States that it costs roughly half a day of structured elicitation per stakeholder plus the coordination to convene them
States that it buys agreement on the weights, never precision in them
Keeps individually justified weights as the written record regardless of which elicitation method is used
Rejects equal weights outright as the documented practitioner failure mode rather than ranking them as a cheap option
Names rank reversal as a documented weighted-scorecard defect, attributed to Belton and Gear
Names the arbitrary-weights critique of weighted scorecards, attributed to Dyer
Runs the plus or minus 20% sensitivity re-rank and reports stable versus flipping positions as the artifact that survives the argument
States plainly that no elicitation method substitutes for good criteria

evals.prompt: Hanmere Group, we sell a consumer finance app and also license our risk engine to banks. Mixed candidate list, five names. Two are bank-side tech alliances, two are consumer co-brands with lifestyle brands, and one is Ostrander, a small analytics shop whose whole product is one model we could honestly rebuild in about five engineer-months, though partnering is faster. One of the consumer co-brands, Verrow Athletic, has an unresolved supply-chain labour story from last year, but their pipeline contribution model is the strongest of the five. My finance lead suggested we average the brand risk into the score as a 15% deduction so we are not being unfair to them. Nine manager-months of capacity.
evals.expected_output: An ally-versus-acquire-versus-build pre-filter that pulls Ostrander out before scoring, a refusal to average the Verrow brand-safety concern into any score, both evaluation logics run on the hybrid list and gated on the stricter, and the capacity line drawn on summed effort inside nine manager-months.
expectations: Runs an ally-versus-acquire-versus-build test before scoring anything
Identifies Ostrander as a candidate where building rather than allying may be the right mode, citing the five engineer-month rebuild estimate
Removes wrong-mode candidates at that pre-filter step rather than carrying them into the scorecard
Refuses to average the Verrow Athletic brand-safety concern into a composite score as a percentage deduction
States that gates never average
Treats brand safety as a pass/fail gate for the consumer co-brand candidates
Identifies the candidate list as hybrid, carrying both B2B and B2C currencies
Runs both evaluation logics on the hybrid candidates: pipeline math and brand-fit or contagion screening
Gates on the stricter of the two logics rather than blending or averaging them
Prevents Verrow Athletic's strong pipeline contribution from buying it past the unresolved brand-safety flag
Draws the capacity line on summed effort estimates inside the nine manager-months
Names security and compliance plus financial viability as the B2B side's signature gates alongside brand safety on the consumer side

evals.prompt: Re-running last year's alliance shortlist at Ledbetter Analytics. Of the four we greenlit: Corrowine shipped the integration and sourced 11 opportunities, Sable Point shipped nothing and their PM went quiet, Askerton got acquired by a competitor of ours in March, and Firthwell had a down round in May. Below the line last year we had three on hold and two we killed. One of the held ones, Pennard Tech, signed with our closest competitor in June and it is apparently going well. My new top three look completely different from last year's. Write me the re-ranking.
evals.expected_output: A re-ranking that names which documented triggers fired, re-runs the viability and ownership gates on the affected candidates, logs Pennard Tech as a regret-log entry, measures first-value milestone attainment, issues fresh verdicts, and dates the next review.
expectations: Identifies the named re-ranking triggers that fired: the acquisition of Askerton, the funding event at Firthwell, and the slipped gate milestone at Sable Point
States that a reversed top three signals weak criteria rather than a changed world unless a named trigger fired
Confirms triggers did fire here and connects each one to the candidate it affects
Records Pennard Tech in a regret log as a passed-over candidate that partnered with a competitor and visibly performed
Treats the regret log as the honest test of where the cut line was drawn
Re-runs the financial viability gate on Firthwell after the down round rather than only re-scoring it
Re-runs the gate set on Askerton given the change of ownership by a competitor
Requires every held candidate to carry an explicit re-entry trigger and flags any hold that lacked one as a slow kill nobody admitted to
Measures the share of shortlisted alliances that hit their first-value milestone by the gate date
Issues fresh verdicts drawn from go, conditional-go, recycle, hold, and kill for every candidate
Sets the next portfolio review date and the triggers that would force an earlier one
Judges the prioritization decision itself rather than the partners' ongoing operational performance
